sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 picks up turn 3: 'I agree with simplifying, but it requires a system.' [s2] T5 answers T4's shrink-the-habit idea: 'remain a passenger to their environment'. [s3] T3 'Both of you are chasing a fragility trap' answers T1 and T2 directly.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns 5, 6 and 8 mostly restate each mind's opening stance; little direct rebuttal. [s2] T3 claims both ignore cues although T1 already proposed an event anchor. [s3] T5 drifts back to Camus's own theme instead of answering T4's never-miss-twice.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 adds that intensity can scale while the habit persists. [s2] T6 adds the clash between wanting control and wanting ease. [s3] T7 adds identity loss as a new cost of the Strategist's volatility plan.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Existentialist's turns 5 and 8 add no new distinctions after turn 2. [s2] T1, T3 and T7 circle the same trigger/small-habit idea. [s3] Turns 6 to 9 mostly restate positions; no new distinction after T7.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 names it: athlete identity versus worker reality. [s2] Ease-minimising vs discipline-building is examined in T4, T5, T6 and T8. [s3] T9 names it: a steady identity habit versus resilience to a volatile schedule.
sub.limitation: [s1] The tension is named in the last turn, not worked through earlier. [s2] The shift-variability problem itself drops away after T3. [s3] T4 never-miss-twice against T6 'do nothing' is never examined.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 folds the Minimalist's simplicity into the Habitualist's system. [s2] T8 Stoic agrees on action over duration, then adds the self-deception worry. [s3] T8 Existentialist reframes acceptance as a chosen act that builds identity.
sub.limitation: [s1] Camus's view never reshapes the other two; it stays parallel. [s2] The Habitualist and Strategist largely merge instead of reshaping each other. [s3] T8 folds into the Habitualist's view instead of reshaping it.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] Section D asks whether the goal is fitness or a sense of control. [s2] T9 sharpens the question to a missing trigger vs a missing reward. [s3] Section D defines consistency as a daily habit or a long-term adaptive pattern.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 9 settles on the Minimalist's own opening position instead of a sharper question. [s2] The reward question appears only in the last turn, undeveloped. [s3] The ending dichotomy (comfort vs resilience) was already stated in Section A.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 engages 'struggle' framing directly: 'If you view it as a struggle, you will quit.' [s2] T5 gives the strongest form of the ease objection: passivity toward the environment. [s3] T4 fairly presses optionality as a possible excuse for doing nothing.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 6 flattens Camus's view of struggle into a recipe for quitting. [s2] T4 says the Stoic 'relies on willpower', a strawman of T2. [s3] T7 misreads the Strategist as 'always tied to high stress'; T6 said train on easy days.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5: identity is fragile when chaos wins. [s2] T6: discipline risks burnout and ease risks avoiding real change; it says why this matters. [s3] T3 argues a fixed schedule is fragile because it 'shatters at the first' shift change.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5's objection gets no answer about how identity survives missed days. [s2] T3's objection is not a real challenge; it restates T1. [s3] T2's 'mechanical life' objection to triggers is rhetorical, not tested.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: [s1] Turn 1's habit-anchoring idea matches Atomic Habits chapter 5. [s2] T8 leans fittingly on Meditations V.1, rising unwillingly to do the work. [s3] Clear's never-miss-twice and Camus's indifferent world are attributed fairly.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 2: 'rebellion against absurd shift hours' stretches Camus; numbered Sisyphus chapters don't exist. [s2] T3 misuses Duhigg's 'keystone habit'; T4's two-minute idea is cited to Ch. 11. [s3] T6 'gain fitness from recovery after high stress' stretches Taleb into training advice.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 hedges: 'The user may fear...' [s2] T8 'I suspect the user fears' is properly hedged. [s3] T5 hedges: 'It is possible you fear the lack of structure.'
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 1 asserts as fact: 'You are failing because you equate a routine...' [s2] T4 states 'willpower is a finite resource' as settled fact. [s3] T1 'You must' and T6's flat prescriptions state preferences as facts.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 concedes 'I agree with simplifying.' [s2] T8 'I agree with the Habitualist on the focus of action over duration'. [s3] T8 says 'My previous stance was too focused on acceptance.'
sub.limitation: [s1] No mind revises a claim; the Existentialist never answers turn 6's objection. [s2] No one answers T6's burnout objection directly. [s3] T6 never answers T4's charge that optionality becomes an excuse.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: [s1] Turn 1 locates the issue: routine tied to a clock time. [s2] T1 'their clock is broken' names the core problem directly. [s3] T1 says the problem is motivation tied to a time the schedule makes impossible.
sub.limitation: [s1] Doesn't separate why they quit: tiredness, planning load, or all-or-nothing thinking. [s2] Never asks why or when the user gives up. [s3] Doesn't ask why the user 'keeps giving up': energy, time, or guilt.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: [s1] Turn 1 ties the cue to the end of a shift. [s2] T3 uses 'walking through the door after a shift' as the cue. [s3] T6 uses shift difficulty to set workout intensity.
sub.limitation: [s1] 'Hang up your uniform' is invented; no night shifts, sleep, or fatigue. [s2] Shift specifics (nights, length, fatigue) barely shape the argument. [s3] Nothing on night shifts, sleep or commute, which shape a shift worker's options.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 serves the stated goal: not fighting your own life. [s2] Section E branches on whether the user values ease or growth. [s3] T9 makes the user choose between steady habit and resilience.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5 pushes the Existentialist's value ('struggle is the point') over the user's goal. [s2] The speakers' values (Stoic growth) are imposed as candidate user values. [s3] The user asked for a routine; the speakers impose identity versus antifragility.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6: 'If you have only ten minutes, do ten minutes.' [s2] T7 allows for one hour or ten minutes, depending on the shift. [s3] T6 'On a brutal shift day, do nothing.'
sub.limitation: [s1] No talk of energy after long or late shifts, or of recovery. [s2] Section E's 'set time regardless of shift' week ignores the user's stated constraint. [s3] Shift-work fatigue and recovery appear only in Section E.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: [s1] Section E gives conditional branches based on what causes anxiety. [s2] T9 makes trigger vs reward a conditional the user can check. [s3] Section E gives conditional branches by priority.
sub.limitation: [s1] Never asks about shift pattern, type of exercise, or why previous attempts stopped. [s2] No turn asks the user for the missing details. [s3] No focused questions about the shift pattern or past failures.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: [s1] Section D: actual fitness or the sense of control? [s2] T6 'want to feel in control, but they also want ease' gives plausible desires. [s3] T9 contrasts the comfort of a steady habit with resilience.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8 declares 'I see a desire for control' as if it were fact. [s2] Section D's 'personal stability' idea never reaches the debate itself. [s3] Desires are the speakers' categories; the user's reasons to exercise are never explored.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 1 brings out the assumption that a routine means a fixed time. [s2] T7 surfaces the assumption that exercise needs a high-intensity block. [s3] T6 challenges the idea that consistency means 'a flat, consistent line.'
sub.limitation: [s1] The all-or-nothing assumption is only implied, never named outright. [s2] The assumption that consistency means daily practice is left unexamined. [s3] The all-or-nothing assumption behind giving up isn't named.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9: athlete identity versus worker reality. [s2] T5 vs T4: ease and resilience as competing valued outcomes. [s3] Section E: mental comfort versus overall fitness and resilience.
sub.limitation: [s1] Doesn't show where these values actually conflict in the user's week. [s2] Health goals themselves are never weighed. [s3] The fitness-vs-comfort framing is asserted, not drawn from the user.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7: fear that doing less means giving up. [s2] T8: a fear that small habits are self-deception, offered without pathologising. [s3] T5 says the frustration stems from feeling a lack of control and from self-judgment.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8 says 'their work controls them' and speculates without hedging. [s2] Guilt over repeated giving up is not named. [s3] No look at outside pressure or shame about repeated failure.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: [s1] Section D's closing question can be taken or left. [s2] Section D asks whether they seek a workout or stability; the user can accept or reject it. [s3] T9: 'The user must decide' which they value.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5 instructs ('Accept that the struggle...') instead of offering a choice. [s2] T2 and T5 prescribe Stoic indifference rather than offering it as a choice. [s3] Offers a binary choice rather than distinctions the user can refine.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] Section E sets out habit-anchoring, minimal action, and reframing. [s2] Section E frames a trigger-based system vs discipline as a training ground. [s3] Section E sets tiny triggers against an opportunistic model.
sub.limitation: [s1] No trial or limited-experiment option is defined. [s2] The discipline option has no concrete form. [s3] No hybrid or minimal-step option, despite T7's micro-habit.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8: a rigid routine breaks under shifting reality. [s2] T6 names the costs of both: burnout vs avoided discomfort. [s3] T7: volatility risks losing the identity of someone who exercises.
sub.limitation: [s1] The cost of minimal sessions, like slower fitness gains, is never stated. [s2] The cost of the small-habit approach (stagnation) is only implied. [s3] The cost of fixed triggers on exhausting days is never weighed.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E: if the system causes more anxiety than exercise, go minimal. [s2] T9: a missing trigger vs a missing reward decides the approach. [s3] Section E: if steady habit matters for mental comfort, adopt tiny triggers.
sub.limitation: [s1] The third branch is vague: 'investigate whether you are seeking...' [s2] The conditions are tied to values, not to observable shift patterns. [s3] Conditions depend on abstract priorities, not observable facts about the shifts.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] Section D notes the identity-versus-acceptance question remains open. [s2] T9 lists willpower, identity or system design as unresolved. [s3] Section A names the comfort-versus-resilience uncertainty.
sub.limitation: [s1] Doesn't name key unknowns like shift length, rest days, or energy. [s2] It does not say which unknown matters most. [s3] Major unknowns like energy, sleep and equipment go unseparated.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: [s1] Turn 1: walk right after the shift ends. [s2] A two-week alternating experiment comparing approaches. [s3] Section E: try both methods for two weeks.
sub.limitation: [s1] No plan for the first week or what to do after a miss. [s2] The 'set time regardless of shift' week may be infeasible for this user. [s3] Tracking 'recovery time' is a vague measure for a habit question.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 is plain: 'Make it effortless.' [s2] T1 'their clock is broken' is plain and apt. [s3] T1's front-door trigger is plain and concrete.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 2's 'rebellion against the absurdity' is abstract for this user. [s2] T5 'indifferent to the external chaos' is abstract. [s3] T3 'optionality' and 'fragility trap' need unpacking.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] Turn 3 addresses both rivals: 'You are both overcomplicating it.' [s2] T4 names the Strategist and the Stoic explicitly when responding. [s3] T9 restates who wants what clearly.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns 3, 7 and 8 switch between 'you' and 'the user/they', which blurs who is addressed. [s2] T3 'Both perspectives ignore' misrepresents what came before. [s3] T7 'that approach' points to a misread version of T6.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] All nine turns fall within 25 to 65 words. [s2] All nine turns fall within 25-65 words and read evenly. [s3] Nine turns, all within 25 to 65 words.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns are evenly paced, so no exchange stands out. [s2] The final reward idea is introduced with no room to develop. [s3] T9 runs long with recap.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] Each mind keeps one clear stance: system, struggle, simplicity. [s2] The Stoic is clearly distinct from the two habit voices. [s3] The three lenses (habit, absurd, antifragile) stay distinct.
sub.limitation: [s1] No mind ever clearly changes position. [s2] Clear and Duhigg overlap heavily; the 'Strategist' title does not match a neurological concern. [s3] The T8 shift is explicit but blurs the Existentialist into the Habitualist.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] Section E condenses the three paths. [s2] T6 adds a new axis instead of repeating. [s3] Turns are tight, with little filler.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8 repeats turn 5's chaos/control point. [s2] T3 and T7 recycle T1's anchor and small-habit point. [s3] Section D partly repeats T9.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8: does work control them? [s2] T6: burnout vs avoidance gives the choice real stakes. [s3] T7 frames identity itself at stake.
sub.limitation: [s1] The stakes of quitting again are never made concrete. [s2] Stakes stay abstract, with no picture of the user's week. [s3] Tension stays conceptual, not tied to a lived moment.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s1] Turn 2's reframe: the problem is wanting predictability. [s2] Section D's stability-not-workout reframe is a mild surprise. [s3] T8 Existentialist reverses toward chosen identity.
sub.limitation: [s1] No reversals after turn 3. [s2] No in-debate reversal or change of mind. [s3] The reversal comes with no pressure that earns it.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] Turn 3's blunt 'You are both overcomplicating it.' [s2] The Stoic's T8 'doing it anyway' has some conviction. [s3] T2's Camus voice: schedule 'does not care about your routine.'
sub.limitation: [s1] The Existentialist sounds generic, not like Camus. [s2] The Strategist has no distinct personality. [s3] The Habitualist's voice is generic coaching.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9: 'no longer fighting your own life.' [s2] T5 'remain a passenger to their environment' is vivid. [s3] T2 pictures the rock rolling back down each time the shift changes.
sub.limitation: [s1] No vivid analogies or images, apart from the uniform. [s2] There are few images or examples beyond walking through the door. [s3] Few other images beyond Sisyphus.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 touches on the fear of giving up. [s2] T8's fear of self-deception adds emotional texture. [s3] T5 moves from defeat to joy in movement.
sub.limitation: [s1] Flat rhythm; the speakers simply rotate with no build. [s2] The rhythm is uniform; there is no build toward T9. [s3] The rhythm is flat; every turn has the same weight.

strengths: [s1] Turn 1 makes the core move: anchor the habit to an event, not a clock time.
[s1] Turns 6-7 give a usable scale-down rule: ten minutes still counts.
[s1] Section D's question, fitness or control, gives real room for reflection.
[s2] Stronger self-discovery: T6's control-vs-ease and T8's fear of self-deception are plausible, non-pathologising desires.
[s2] Section D's question, workout or stability the job denies, is a reflective reframe the user can own.
[s2] T5 sharpens the Stoic objection to shrinking habits: 'remain a passenger to their environment'.
[s3] Three clearly distinct lenses, with T2's Sisyphus image making the frustration vivid
[s3] T6 to T7 surfaces a real tension: adaptive intensity versus a stable exercise identity
[s3] T5 names fear and self-judgment in hedged terms
weaknesses: [s1] The Existentialist (turns 2, 5, 8) loosely paraphrases Camus and never answers turn 6's objection.
[s1] Ignores shift-work realities: fatigue, sleep, night shifts; 'uniform' detail is invented (turn 1).
[s1] Turns 3, 7, 8 talk about 'the user' in third person and state motives as fact.
[s2] The Habitualist and Strategist overlap: T3 restates T1 while claiming both missed the cue.
[s2] Grounding slips: T3 misuses 'keystone habit', and T4 asserts finite willpower as fact with a wrong chapter.
[s2] Section E's 'set time regardless of shift' week contradicts the user's stated constraint.
[s3] T7 Habitualist misreads T6 as exercise 'always tied to high stress'
[s3] T4 never-miss-twice versus T6 'do nothing' left unresolved and unanswered
[s3] No questions about the shift pattern; Section E's 'recovery time' test is vague
editorNotes: [s1] Require each turn after the third to answer a specific earlier claim by turn number or quote.
[s1] Require the debate to raise at least two concrete constraints from the situation (energy, sleep, timing) without inventing details.
[s1] Require speakers to address the user only as 'you' and to hedge any claim about the user's motives.
[s1] Require at least one mind to concede or revise a claim on the page.
[s2] Require three minds with clearly non-overlapping methods; reject two authors from the same subgenre.
[s2] Require any next-step experiment to be feasible under the user's stated constraints.
[s2] Have the role title match the mind's stated concern and book.
[s2] Require each challenge to quote or paraphrase accurately what the opponent actually said before rebutting it.
[s3] Require a speaker to restate the opponent's claim before rebutting it, to stop misreads like T7.
[s3] Require one turn or Section E to ask two focused questions about the user's shift pattern and energy.
[s3] Require Section E's test to measure the behaviour in question, such as sessions done, not proxies.

sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 answers turn 6 directly: 'It matters because...' [s2] T4 takes up Meadows' weekly volume and answers with a tiered daily minimum. [s3] T4 answers T3's internal-character point with 'willpower is a limited resource.'
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 3 does not engage turn 2's Sartre claim. [s2] T2 ignores T1's event-anchor idea; opens with a generic Stoic stance. [s3] T9 Stoic restates duty rather than answering T7's two-tier plan.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 sorts the rivals' assumptions: system, identity, health. [s2] Moves from anchors (T1) to weekly volume (T3), tiers (T4), buffer (T6), energy variable (T9). [s3] T7 adds the two-tier high-energy plan and low-energy fallback.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns 8-9 open new themes instead of building on turn 7. [s2] Stoic turns T5/T8 restate the control thesis without adding mechanics. [s3] T5 to T6 repeat the opening split before moving forward.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8: wanting both security and spontaneity, which can't fully coexist. [s2] T6 'Values do not move muscles' sets willpower against system design. [s3] T12: logistical failure, or failure to accept their life as it is?
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 7's decision-fatigue point versus turn 6's 'why does it matter' is never resolved. [s2] Daily cue vs weekly volume tension (T3/T4) is raised and then dropped. [s3] Discipline versus flexibility is named more than examined.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 builds on the Stoic: 'I agree with the Stoic, but...' [s2] T7 folds Meadows' buffer into friction reduction; T8 concedes environment prep. [s3] T7 and T8 merge cue and capacity into one compromise.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Existentialist stays separate and never takes up the Architect's gear tactic. [s2] The Stoic never engages weekly volume or tiers concretely. [s3] T8 agrees quickly; the synthesis isn't stress-tested.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] Section D: the discomfort is predictability versus flux. [s2] T9 sharpens the question: is failure about time or energy recovery? [s3] T12 narrows to how they respond on days they miss.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 9 drifts into abstraction instead of sharpening the practical question. [s2] Section D's 'measuring recovery' rests on one closing turn, not the debate. [s3] Section D leaves the discipline-versus-logistics split loosely defined.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5 grants the gear idea before objecting: 'a fine tactic, but...' [s2] T4 grants Meadows' feedback-loop point before objecting on immediate wins. [s3] T6 takes T5's flexibility seriously and names its risk: mood choosing comfort.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 6 reduces the Existentialist to 'wants an identity.' [s2] T6 reduces the Stoic to willpower, which T5 did not claim. [s3] T2 caricatures triggers as rigid enough to 'cause burnout.'

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 asks why clock time matters if the goal is health. [s2] T4: weekly goals lose immediate reward, a real mechanism objection. [s3] T5: exercising at low energy breeds resentment rather than engagement.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8's claim that rigidity causes unhappiness gets no reply. [s2] T2 'that is a mistake' is asserted without reasons tied to shift work. [s3] T3 'Both of you focus on external conditions' sidesteps the practical question.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: [s1] Turn 3 quotes the Enchiridion's opening line faithfully, with pd=true. [s2] T5's 'body is external' faithfully tracks Enchiridion 1 and 9. [s3] Epictetus on control and Csikszentmihalyi on matching challenge are apt.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 7's 'drains your willpower' treats contested ego-depletion research as settled. [s2] T6 calls setting out gear a Meadows 'buffer'/'delay', a loose misuse of terms. [s3] T4 'willpower is a limited resource' is contested; T5 'highest form of mastery' isn't Flow.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] Turn 2 hedges with 'perhaps.' [s2] T9 flags fatigue as an unmeasured variable rather than asserting a cause. [s3] T11 hedges: 'I suspect they believe' failure is total.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 2 then says 'They must realize'; turn 4 says 'you will always default to rest.' [s2] T7 asserts the user has 'habits of avoidance'; T8 'will always find an excuse'. [s3] T10 asserts 'The user clearly fears' with no evidence.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 concedes the Stoic's point before adding implementation. [s2] T8 'I concede that preparing the environment helps' and then refines. [s3] T8 'That is a better compromise'; T9 'I concede that structure helps.'
sub.limitation: [s1] No speaker revises their own claim after it is challenged. [s2] No mind revises its core claim; the concessions stay at the edges. [s3] T9's concession comes with a retreat to an unargued 'core issue.'

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: [s1] Turn 1: the habit is attached to a clock. [s2] T1 reframes the need for a fixed time as the user's assumption. [s3] T1 says the user assumes a routine needs a fixed clock time.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 2 suggests the user defines themselves as unable to commit, which is unsupported. [s2] Never asks what 'giving up' looks like, or after how long. [s3] Never asks what giving up actually looks like for them.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4: prepare gym gear before the shift starts. [s2] T1 anchors to 'finishing a shift', which uses the shift-work detail. [s3] T1 ties the cue to taking off the work uniform.
sub.limitation: [s1] No talk of shift length, night work, or tiredness after work. [s2] Shift type (nights, rotating) and the commute go unused. [s3] Uniform detail is invented; no night-shift or sleep considerations.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 holds to the user's likely goal: health. [s2] T3 weekly volume fits the user's wish for a schedule-independent routine. [s3] Section A: a desire for consistency against unpredictable hours.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5 imposes the 'athlete' identity, which the user never mentioned. [s2] The user's own fitness goal is never asked about or used. [s3] T9's 'duty they owe themselves' imposes the Stoic's value.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 counts the job's flexibility as a real cost. [s2] T9 names energy recovery as a constraint of rotating shifts. [s3] T2: a grueling shift makes a rigid trigger risky.
sub.limitation: [s1] Doesn't address limited time or energy on heavy weeks. [s2] Circadian disruption and sleep after night shifts get no specific treatment. [s3] Time, sleep and recovery constraints of rotating shifts are untouched.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: [s1] Section E: track whether time or motivation is missing. [s2] Section E branches on exhaustion vs all-or-nothing vs unknown. [s3] Section E branches on why the user abandons exercise.
sub.limitation: [s1] No direct questions about how past attempts ended. [s2] No focused question to the user appears inside the debate turns. [s3] No direct question to the user inside the debate.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 separates a system, an identity, and health. [s2] T8 contrasts exercise as a task with exercise as an expression of character. [s3] Section D: security of a rigid schedule versus flexibility.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 2 presents a self-sabotage motive with little hedging. [s2] Never asks why the user wants to exercise at all. [s3] T10 states the desire as fact rather than as one possibility.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6: 'Stop judging the irregularity as a failure.' [s2] T1 surfaces the assumption that a fixed clock time is required. [s3] T11 exposes the false binary that falling short of the ideal intensity counts as total failure.
sub.limitation: [s1] Doesn't examine whether 'routine' must mean daily. [s2] The all-or-nothing assumption appears only in Section E, not in the debate. [s3] T1's fixed-clock assumption is asserted, not offered for reflection.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 sets security against spontaneity. [s2] T5 defines success as acting on values even when the workout is shortened. [s3] T6 and T9 weigh comfort against self-mastery.
sub.limitation: [s1] Doesn't ask which of those the user actually ranks higher. [s2] Conflicting priorities (rest vs movement) are not set against each other for the user. [s3] The user's own reasons for exercising are never surfaced.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9: the routine as a security blanket against uncertainty. [s2] Section D suggests the user may conflate discipline with rigidity. [s3] T12 points to self-talk on the days they miss.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5's 'already choosing by not exercising' risks blame. [s2] Guilt and the sense of failure from 'keep giving up' go unaddressed. [s3] T10 'clearly fears' declares a hidden fact.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 asks: 'What is lost if you abandon...?' [s2] T9's time vs energy question is one the user can test and own. [s3] T12 leaves an open question about their response to misses.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 2's 'They must realize' closes options instead of opening them. [s2] T7/T8 hand down verdicts about the user instead of offering questions. [s3] Speakers talk about 'the user' rather than inviting them.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] Section E: event trigger versus daily reframe. [s2] Options: event anchor, weekly volume, tiered minimum, recovery-first rule. [s3] Section E sets a minimum viable trigger routine against an energy-matched approach.
sub.limitation: [s1] Leaves out a scaled-down minimum-session option. [s2] Options are never laid side by side as a choice. [s3] T7's hybrid isn't carried into Section E as an option.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8: choosing rigidity limits flexibility. [s2] T4: weekly totals absorb variability but lose the daily reward. [s3] T4 versus T5: offloading decisions versus resentment at low energy.
sub.limitation: [s1] The cost of event-anchoring on chaotic days isn't covered. [s2] The tiered and recovery-first options are presented as free of cost. [s3] The costs of the two-tier plan are never stated.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E: if decision fatigue, use triggers; if fear of losing control, reframe. [s2] Section E: exhaustion points to recovery-first; mindset points to habit-anchoring. [s3] Section E: abandon over a missed slot, or over exhaustion?
sub.limitation: [s1] The conditions aren't tied to shift details. [s2] No condition that would favour weekly volume over daily anchors. [s3] The conditions are plausible but not tied to shift data.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] Section E's tracking test targets the consequential unknown. [s2] T9 separates the consequential unknown: time vs energy. [s3] Section E flags not knowing if they're too hard on themselves.
sub.limitation: [s1] Smaller unknowns, like workout type, aren't set apart. [s2] Minor unknowns (gym access, kind of exercise) are not ranked. [s3] Doesn't rank which unknown matters most.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4: prepare gear; turn 1: anchor to waking or end of shift. [s2] Two-week tracking of energy against shift start times to find a 'dead zone'. [s3] T7's two routines; Section E says to track self-talk after a missed day.
sub.limitation: [s1] No minimum version for exhausting days. [s2] No concrete minimum workout or first-week action is given. [s3] No first concrete action for this week's schedule.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6: '5 AM or 5 PM?' is concrete. [s2] T3 'total volume of movement over the week' is plain and concrete. [s3] T7's high-energy and low-energy routines are easy to grasp.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 5's 'anxiety of choice' and 'creates the athlete' are abstract. [s2] T6 'delay mechanism that stores energy' is jargon left unclear. [s3] T6 'tyranny of their own desires' is abstract.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 names 'The Architect' and 'the Existentialist' explicitly. [s2] T4 names Meadows and states exactly which point it accepts. [s3] T10 states what is being debated: a fixed time or a fixed trigger.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 2 refers to 'the user' in third person. [s2] T2 'They could say' leaves unclear who 'they' are. [s3] T8 'That is a better compromise' leaves the comparison implicit.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] Turns run about 35 to 50 words, all within limits. [s2] All nine turns fall within 25-65 words; even rhythm. [s3] Twelve turns, all within limits and short.
sub.limitation: [s1] The closing turns are no shorter or sharper. [s2] Nine turns leave little room to resolve the volume-vs-cue thread. [s3] T8 is barely above the minimum and adds little.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] The three stances are distinct: cues, choice, control. [s2] Habit, Stoic and Systems lenses stay clearly separate throughout. [s3] The Stoic's control lens stands apart.
sub.limitation: [s1] No explicit change of position. [s2] Changes of position are small and seldom flagged. [s3] The Habit Architect and Flow Strategist converge by T10 and T11.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] Little repetition across the nine turns. [s2] T7 recasts the buffer as friction reduction without restating it. [s3] Little repetition in turns 1 to 7.
sub.limitation: [s1] Section D repeats turn 8's tension without adding to it. [s2] T8 repeats T5's character-over-circumstance point. [s3] T9 and T12 restate the Stoic's frustration theme.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5: 'already choosing by not exercising.' [s2] T6 'I must challenge the Stoic' gives real friction over willpower. [s3] T6: mood will 'eventually opt for comfort.'
sub.limitation: [s1] The stakes stay abstract; no picture of a failed week. [s2] The cost of failing, to health or self-trust, is never made vivid. [s3] Stakes stay abstract; nothing for the user to lose is named.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 reframes the routine as a security blanket. [s2] T9 recasts the problem as energy recovery, a mild turn. [s3] T9 Stoic concedes structure helps.
sub.limitation: [s1] No speaker is moved by another. [s2] No mind is genuinely moved off its position. [s3] Predictable convergence with no twist.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] The Stoic's terse questions in turns 6 and 9. [s2] The Systems Thinker's bluntness in T3 'You are both ignoring' has edge. [s3] Stoic Sage has some gravity in T6.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Architect's voice is mostly bullet-point advice. [s2] The Stoic voice is generic and not recognisably Epictetan. [s3] Voices are textbook summaries, flat in register.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9's 'security blanket against the uncertainty of life.' [s2] T6 'Values do not move muscles' is the one sharp line. [s3] T1's cue of taking off the work uniform.
sub.limitation: [s1] Few concrete images beyond gear and clock times. [s2] No concrete scene of a shift worker coming home exhausted. [s3] No analogy or image that sticks.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] It builds from tactics (turn 4) to fear (turn 9). [s2] The T9 open question leaves something to be resolved. [s3] T12 ends on an open, personal question.
sub.limitation: [s1] Middle turns 5-8 keep one even intensity. [s2] Intensity stays flat from T1 to T8. [s3] Even tempo throughout; little emotional rise.

strengths: [s1] Turn 6 sorts the rivals' hidden assumptions, and turn 7 answers it directly.
[s1] Turn 3 quotes the Enchiridion faithfully, with pd=true, and applies it to the schedule.
[s1] Section E's tracking test (time versus motivation) is a usable diagnostic.
[s2] Concrete mechanisms that build on each other: event anchor, weekly volume, tiered minimum, prepared gear (T1-T7).
[s2] T9 and Section E turn the dispute into a testable time-vs-energy question with a two-week tracking step.
[s2] Real concessions: T4 grants the feedback loop and T8 grants environment design, each then refined.
[s3] T7 gives a concrete two-tier plan with a uniform-based cue
[s3] T11 and T12 surface the all-or-nothing belief and responses to missed days
[s3] Section E branches on observable reasons the user abandons exercise
weaknesses: [s1] Turn 2 (Existentialist) suggests self-sabotage without evidence and says 'They must realize.'
[s1] No minimum-dose option for exhausting shifts; fatigue and sleep are never raised.
[s1] Turn 7 states willpower depletion as fact; turn 8's rigidity claim is never challenged.
[s2] The Stoic Practitioner (T2, T5, T8) repeats control-over-externals and never engages the concrete systems.
[s2] Calibration: T7's 'habits of avoidance' and T8's 'will always find an excuse' are asserted about the user.
[s2] Self-discovery is thin: no turn asks why the user wants to exercise or what failing feels like.
[s3] T10 Habit Architect asserts 'The user clearly fears' as fact
[s3] T4's 'willpower is a limited resource' and T5's 'highest form of mastery' are weakly grounded
[s3] Flat voices and little drama; T8 agrees too quickly
editorNotes: [s1] Require hedged, conditional language for any claim about the user's motives; ban 'must realize.'
[s1] Require at least one concrete fallback plan for low-energy or irregular days.
[s1] Require each mind's last turn to revise or concede something raised against it.
[s1] Prompt minds to flag contested empirical claims, such as willpower depletion, as interpretations.
[s2] Require one turn that asks the user a focused question about motive or what 'giving up' looks like.
[s2] Make each mind change something concrete in response to an opponent, not just restate its doctrine.
[s2] Forbid assertions about the user's psychology unless framed as a hypothesis the user can check.
[s2] Ask for one vivid concrete scenario drawn from the user's situation, for example coming home after a night shift.
[s3] Require claims about the user's inner states to be hedged as possibilities, with a check they can run.
[s3] Have the editor drop contested science claims like ego depletion, or flag them as uncertain.
[s3] Ask each mind for one vivid, situation-specific image or example to lift engagement.
